owned by w02c-p15-028 (readonly unit of this packet): preserve the source's hypotheses on the data of definition (8.1) and the remark that weakens them: the convention that every singular sentence of L expresses a potential datum, and note 33 (data cover actual as well as potential data; the convention is plausible especially when the primitives name directly observable attributes, each singular sentence then describing a logically possible state of affairs ascertainable by observation; that observability assumption is not essential for the definition and formal theory of sections 8 and 9), p. 165. Also absent are the justificatory claims the definition explicates: theories compared by explanatory or predictive power, a powerful theory deriving many data from little initial information, and systematic power reflected in the ratio of the information derivable by means of T to the initial information required (p. 164); and the stated reason, generality and simplicity, for letting T be any sentence (p. 165). The route has the definition (systematic-power.tex lines 89 to 108), the convention that T may be any sentence (lines 18 to 19) and the deductive-systematization starting point (w02b-p15-025 lines 48 to 57 and 322 to 324) only.

owned by w02c-p15-028 (readonly unit of this packet): supply the source's justificatory and historical claims attached to r1 and g1: that range and content vary inversely (the more a sentence asserts, the smaller the variety of its possible realizations), that content counts are normalized to the interval from 0 to 1, and that the content of a finite class K is g1 of the conjunction of K (p. 169); and the report that Carnap showed r1 gives the probability p1 characteristics incompatible with the intended meaning of logical probability ([Inductive Logic] pp. 80 to 81, n. 39), for which reason Carnap and Helmer with Hempel and Oppenheim proposed other range measures (p. 170). The routed entry (systematic-power.tex lines 127 to 137) has formulas (9.1), (9.4) and (9.5) only; w02b-p15-025 lines 325 to 326 add only that r1 weights every assignment equally; systematic-power.tex lines 394 to 398 disclaim any reproduction of Carnap's measure.

owned by w02c-p15-028 (readonly unit of this packet): preserve the source's variants of logical probability and its evaluation of the generalized measure: Carnap's r2 (a specified weight for each maximal sentence, not all equal; the range of a singular sentence as the sum over its constituent maximal sentences; p2(T,S) = r2(T.S)/r2(S) for singular T and S) and n. 38 (p defined for certain cases as a limit, [Inductive Logic] p. 75, which the authors set aside), p. 170; note 40 in full (the Helmer, Hempel and Oppenheim range measure r_I relative to empirical information I; dc(T,S) undefined in certain cases with generalized S, as McKinsey pointed out; dc failing some theorems of elementary probability theory; its methodologically desirable features; the suggested but unpursued systematic-power concept built from r_I), pp. 170 to 171; the remark that (9.9) defines s for every S with g(S) not 0 whereas the section 8 definition was restricted to singular, not formally true S (p. 172); and the closing claims that the generalized concept, the dual counterpart of logical probability, yields a simpler and more comprehensive theory than the initial definition, and that both theories are purely formal, their application needing solutions to problems about the logical structure of the language of science and the interpretation of its concepts, with the recent investigations of n. 41 (Goodman; Carnap) (p. 173). On the route appear only the definitions (systematic-power.tex lines 243 to 258), the limiting extension, the information-dependence of dc and its not being a probability in the strict sense (w02b-p15-025 lines 399 to 404), and the two open problems (systematic-power.tex lines 444 to 452; w02b-p15-025 lines 393 to 397).

owned by w02c-p15-028 (readonly unit of this packet): write the steps of the converse transformation that the theorem states (systematic-power.tex line 328) and that source (9.13) asserts (p. 173): for a universally valid equality or inequality in s_r terms, show that each p_r(D(B),D(C)) equals s_r(B(not A_1, ..., not A_m), C(not A_1, ..., not A_m)), that r(D(C)) equals g(C(not A_1, ..., not A_m)) so definedness transfers, and that substituting the negated metavariables yields the p_r statement.
